It's December. Mrs Hoffmann has grown weak since the pneumonia and Mara now visits her every day. One evening, the old pianist takes a yellowed envelope out of a drawer.
Mara, please open the top drawer. Right at the back there's an envelope. Yes, the yellow one.
It's very old. What is it?
A letter I never sent. From 1961. I wish I had sent it back then.

To Friedrich. Friedrich Mertens. He was a violinist. We studied together, at the Conservatory. He lived in the West, in Charlottenburg, I lived in the East. Back then it wasn't a problem. You simply took the S-Bahn back and forth.

Until the thirteenth of August 1961. The evening before, we had played together. He walked me to the S-Bahn and said: see you Monday. On Sunday the border was closed. It was as if someone had cut the city in two with a knife.

I wrote it a week later. But I was afraid. Letters to the West were opened and read. My father had just died, and my mother was on her own. So I put it in the drawer. And there it has been for sixty-five years.
You never heard from him again?

Once. In 1975 I heard a concert from Vienna on the radio. The announcer said: the soloist is Friedrich Mertens. I pretended I didn't care. My mother was sitting next to me. Then I went into the kitchen and cried.
If only I'd known that earlier…
And what would you have done, child? More than sixty years have passed. He's surely no longer alive. I just wanted someone to read the letter one day. Before I… well. Read it. Please.
“so getan, als ob” = I pretended that
“ZAYN-zookht”: a famous German word, roughly “longing” or “yearning”.
When you wish for something that is NOT reality right now, you use the Konjunktiv II. Two forms:
Ich wünschte, ich hätte mehr Zeit.
Wenn ich doch mehr Zeit hätte!
If only I had more time!
If only I had more time!
If only it were spring already!
For things in the past you wish had been different: hätte / wäre + participle:
If only I had come earlier!
“doch” and “nur” can't be translated exactly; they strengthen the wish, like “if only” or “oh, if…” in English.
Unreal comparisons (as if) are made with the Konjunktiv II:
Sie spielt, als ob sie zwanzig wäre.
Er spricht, als wenn er alles wüsste.
Sie spielt, als wäre sie zwanzig.
It was as if someone had cut the city in two.
You look as if you hadn't slept.
“so tun, als ob / als” = to pretend that:
He pretends he hasn't heard anything.
Don't pretend you don't know me! (in speech, sometimes with the indicative too)

The letter was written in ink, in a fine, slanting hand that Mara recognised at once, although it was younger and firmer than the handwriting on the notes Mrs Hoffmann wrote her nowadays. The paper was yellowed and soft as fabric at the corners. Mara read it slowly, aloud, while Mrs Hoffmann sat in her armchair with her eyes closed.

“Dear Friedrich, I don't know whether this letter will ever reach you. I don't even know whether I'll have the courage to send it. For a week now I've been standing on Bernauer Straße every evening, looking across to the other side. I pretend I'm just walking by. In reality I'm looking for your face in every window. I wish I had said something other than ‘see you Monday’ to you at the station. I wish I had told you what I've been feeling for two years.”

“If only I had stayed with you that night! Then I would be on your side now. But my mother is alone, my father is dead, and I can't leave her. I play our sonata every evening, alone, and it sounds as if half of it were missing. And it is. If you read this letter, then now you know: I loved you. I will always love you. Your Grete.”

When Mara had finished, the room was silent for a long time. Outside it was snowing. Mrs Hoffmann opened her eyes. She wasn't crying. She was smiling, very slightly, as if she had just put down a heavy bag she had carried for sixty-five years. “Thank you, child,” she said. “Now someone has read it.”

Then she stood up slowly, leaned on Mara's arm and went to the piano. She put an old, worn volume of sheet music on the stand. “Sonata for violin and piano”, it said, “Johannes Brahms, No. 1, G major”. Next to it, in pencil, in the same slanting hand: “F. & G., summer 1961”. She played only the piano part. It sounded exactly as she had written in the letter: as if half of it were missing. In some places she paused, as if she were waiting for a violin that didn't come. Mara sat on the sofa and hardly dared to breathe. Down in the courtyard, Kuba stopped with Bruno and looked up. On the first floor, Ludwig opened his window, although it was December and very cold.

Mara couldn't sleep that night. At eleven she called Andrei, who was sitting on the sofa in Mara's living room studying for his master's. She told him everything. Andrei listened without interrupting her. Then he said: “Mara. What if he's still alive?”
He'd have to be over ninety. Mrs Hoffmann says he's surely no longer alive.

Mrs Hoffmann is ninety-three and plays Chopin every evening. Ludwig is eighty-one and drives the tram. People live a long time in this house. I study computer science, Mara. If there's a trace anywhere, I'll find it.

Andrei searched for three weeks. He searched old concert programmes, orchestra archives, newspaper articles from Vienna, Hamburg and Zurich. He found Friedrich Mertens as a soloist in Vienna in 1975, as first violinist in an orchestra in Hamburg in the eighties, as a teacher at the Conservatory in Lübeck until 2001. And then, shortly before Christmas, he found a short news item on the website of a music society in Lübeck: “Our honorary member Friedrich Mertens is celebrating his 95th birthday. He still teaches two pupils every Wednesday in his house on the banks of the Trave.”

Andrei was sitting in Mara's room in the middle of the night, with his laptop in his hand, and he woke her up. Mara read the news item three times. Then she sat bolt upright and looked at him as if she had seen a ghost. “He's alive,” she whispered. “He's alive, Andrei.”

The next morning, Mara went to Ludwig. She needed advice. Should she tell Mrs Hoffmann? What would happen if she got upset? What would happen if Friedrich had forgotten her? What would happen if he was married, had children, grandchildren, a whole life in which there was no longer any room for Grete?

Mara. You once told me not to wait too long. With Thomas. And you were right. Margarete is ninety-three. If you wait now, you may wait too long. And then you'll wish for the rest of your life that you had done it.

In the evening, Mara told Jakob everything, over a cup of tea in his small flat on Oderberger Straße, among piles of exercise books and the cello in the corner. Jakob listened and then said something Mara hadn't thought of. “You don't have to tell Friedrich about Mrs Hoffmann yourself,” he said. “You can simply send him the letter. A copy. With three words from you. Then he decides for himself what he wants to do. Sixty-five years too late. But not too late.”

On 23 December, Mara took an envelope to the post office on Kollwitzplatz. In it was a copy of the 1961 letter and a little note on which she had written, in her most beautiful German handwriting: “She's alive. Kastanienallee 31, fourth floor. She plays every evening at nine.” When the envelope dropped into the yellow postbox, it was as if she herself had waited sixty-five years.

Christmas came and went. Once again everyone sat at Ludwig's under the yellow lamp, this time with Jakob, who brought his cello and played with Paul and Ludwig until the neighbours below knocked on the ceiling, not because it was too loud, but because they wanted to sing along. Mrs Hoffmann was once again carried down the stairs on a chair, this time by Andrei and Jakob. She was more cheerful than Mara had seen her in months. Mara told her nothing about the envelope. Every morning she checked the letterbox before leaving for work. Every morning it was empty, apart from bills and advertising. On 30 December, at ten in the morning, someone knocked at her door. It was the postman, with a parcel for the fourth floor. “The old lady isn't opening,” he said. “Can you take it? It's from Lübeck.”

Mara took the parcel. It was long and narrow, wrapped in brown paper, and it wasn't heavy. Under sender it said, in old, shaky handwriting: “F. Mertens, An der Trave 12, Lübeck”. Mara stood in the hallway for a long time, holding the parcel in both hands, and didn't dare go up the stairs.
